s: is_made_of Raphia palm [its ribs] The Basongo Meno have made fishing-traps from Raphia-palm ribs since the earliest times. While constructing one, a man produced fire by boring a hole in one of its ribs.

l: boring a hole in a Raphia rib, The Library
s: elicits fire [when performed with a pointed stick] A man boring a hole in the end of a Raphia-palm rib with a small pointed stick elicited fire. The Basongo Meno have used this method of procuring fire ever since.

l: Sky God Obassi Osaw, The Library
s: Obassi Osaw, a Sky God in the Ekoi account, made everything at the world's beginning and lived in a sky house, keeping fire with his wives. He withheld fire from earth until the Lame Boy stole it, then sent his eldest son.
Etim ‘Ne is a chief of the people on earth who sends Lame Boy to ask Obassi Osaw for fire; after the failure, he humbles himself before the Sky God but returns without fire.

Lame Boy is a boy who first asks Obassi Osaw for fire and is refused. He serves the Sky God, steals a fire-brand from the house of the god's wives, wraps it in plantain leaves and his cloth, and brings fire to earth. Akpan punishes him by making him unable to walk, and he becomes lame.
The Lengua Indians of the Paraguayan Chaco originally lacked fire and ate raw food until an Indian stole burning sticks from a bird and shared fire with his people.
The thunder-bird kindled fire to cook snails, but Indians stole it. In anger it created a thunderstorm and lightning to punish them, then had to eat its food raw ever since.
The Tapietes, originally without fire, gained it when a frog stole two sparks from the black vulture and carried them to them.
The black vulture possessed fire obtained from lightning before the Tapietes had any; after the frog stole two sparks, it lacked fire, wept, and sat with its hands over its head.

steals fire [two sparks from the black vulture's fire] The frog stole two sparks from the black vulture’s fire and brought them in its mouth to the Tapietes. This theft gave the Tapietes fire and deprived the black vulture of it.

extract fire [from trees by friction] The Tembes lacked fire and had to dry their meat in the sun. They tried to steal fire from the king vulture and eventually obtained a fire-brand, which they used to put fire into the trees from which they extract it by friction.
The king vulture formerly possessed fire and used it to roast maggots at a tapir carcass with its clan, until an old medicine-man snatched a fire-brand for the Tembes.

lack fire [before obtaining it from mutug] The Arekuna Indians tell of a time when people had no fire and ate food raw. Makunaima and his brothers followed a string tied to the mutug’s tail to its house and carried fire away.
Makunaima is a man who lived with his brothers before the great flood; lacking fire, he tied a string to mutug’s tail, followed it to a bird’s house, and helped take fire.
Mutug is a little green bird, identified as Prionites momola, said in Loango to possess fire while fishing; Makunaima followed a string tied to its tail to its house, where fire was taken.

lack fire [in the beginning] The Tarumas say that the first woman secretly produced fire from her genital canal after the elder brother forced her to reveal her secret. Their account also explains how several animals were burned or altered while attempting to take or step on the fire.
Duid, the younger of two brothers before there was a woman, fishes the first woman from a deep pool, marries her, and later possesses the fire she reveals.

identify iguana [as former possessor of fire] The Cora Indians say that the iguana carried fire to the sky after quarreling with his wife and mother-in-law. Several birds failed to retrieve it, but the opossum succeeded in bringing fire down, after which the people kept it.
Iguana, a lizard, possessed fire but, after quarreling with his wife and mother-in-law, retired to the sky with it, leaving people on earth without fire.

steals fire [from an old man in the sky] The opossum climbed to the sky in the Cora account and found an old man sitting by a fire. It seized a fire-brand, dragged it toward the way down, and dropped it when overtaken, causing the earth to catch fire.

identify creator [as Spider] The Sia Indians say that people originally had no fire and grew tired of eating grass like deer. They sent Coyote to steal fire from Spider’s underground house, and Coyote returned with a burning cedar brand tied to his tail.
The Navahoes, a human group, lacked fire when men first emerged from the earth; animals possessed it until Coyote, Bat, and Squirrel stole and passed it to them.

learn fire-making by friction [from Coyote] The Uintah Utes tell of Coyote and other animals searching for fire among people who possessed it. Coyote stole the fire and passed it among Eagle, Humming-bird, Hawk-Moth, Chicken-Hawk, and others until it reached his people in a sagebrush tube.

lack fire [in the early ages of the world] The Karok Indians say that the Creator hid fire and gave it to two old hags to guard. Coyote stole it and passed it along animal runners; the ground-squirrel was burned while carrying it, and a frog lost its tail when an old hag pursued the thieves.
Thunder keeps all fire in his house under Woswosim’s guard; Mouse steals it while the guard sleeps, and Skunk kills Thunder during his pursuit.

The Nootkas are one of the Vancouver Island tribes. After twins’ birth, they observe extensive regulations: seclusion in a distant woods hut, bathing, painted faces, ritual songs, and restrictions involving fresh food and salmon. Twins and their father are believed to attract salmon, promising a good salmon year.

The Tsimshian are an adjacent coastal tribe in British Columbia who believe twins’ wishes are fulfilled; twins can call salmon and olachen, are called Sewthan, “making plentiful,” and are feared for harming enemies.

Coyote is the first thief of fire in a Thompson Indians myth. Wearing a headdress of combustible shavings, Coyote dances around a fire, flees when it ignites, and passes fire along a chain of animals to Fox, Wolf, and Antelope.

British Columbia is a region associated with Bella Coola and Kwakiutl Indians and the interior home of Thompson Indians. It is also the setting for fire myths of Lillooet, Okanaken, and Chilcotin Indians and Sun-story versions told by several groups.
Eagle assists Beaver in stealing fire from the sky people by diverting their attention while Beaver carries the fire away.

Haida Indians inhabit Queen Charlotte Islands and tell that Raven stole fire, daylight, fresh water, and olachen fish from a chief or deity, carrying fire as a burning brand and giving these benefits to mankind.
Tlingit Indians inhabit Alaska. In accounts of fire’s origin, Raven brings it from an island or sends animals to Snow-Owl; Deer succeeds by carrying burning fir-wood on his tail, leaving it stumpy.

protects wren [through beliefs against killing or robbing its nest] In Normandy, people say that the wren fetched fire from heaven after the larger birds refused. The wren's feathers burned, so the other birds gave it feathers, while the screech-owl refused and was thereafter attacked and forced to hide by day.

Wren, respected in Normandy, offers and succeeds in fetching fire from heaven; its feathers burn on the return, and other birds replace them, leaving speckled plumage. The myth is also told in Brittany.

uses chain of animals [in American fire myths] The theft of fire is attributed to animals such as Coyote, Beaver, Raven, and the wren in different traditions. The stolen fire is carried from its guarded location to mankind or passed along a chain of animals.

The unit presents myths about the origin of fire in which animals obtain it from chiefs, deities, Snow-Owl, the sky, heaven, or distant islands. These myths also explain why wood and stones contain fire and why animals have distinctive features caused by carrying or stealing it.
Neleus, son of Poseidon and father of Pero, promises Pero to whoever recovers Phylacus’s kine; Melampus brings the kine to Pylus as her bridal gift.
is_a place in Thessaly [where Melampus sought the cows] Othrys was the place to which Melampus went to get the kine. Watchmen and herdsmen caught him there and handed him over to Iphiclus.

are_consulted_about Iphiclus's cure [at Melampus's sacrifice] Melampus sacrificed an ox and distributed portions to the birds, asking whether any knew how Iphiclus could have children. The birds were initially unable to answer, and the vulture was summoned to provide the explanation.
Vulture succeeds where other birds cannot, telling Melampus that a knife in a wild pear-tree causes Iphiclus's childlessness and prescribing rust in wine for ten days; it also eats Tityus's heart.

is_stuck_in wild pear-tree [by Phylacus] Phylacus used the knife while pursuing Iphiclus and then stuck it into a wild pear-tree. According to one account, the knife accidentally touched Iphiclus's genitals, and its rust was later used to cure his childlessness.

contains knife [the knife used in Iphiclus's cure] The wild pear-tree received the knife that Phylacus had used while pursuing Iphiclus. The knife remained enclosed by the tree's bark until it was recovered for Iphiclus's cure.

l: rust of the knife, The Library
s: cures Iphiclus's cure [through sympathetic or homoeopathic magic] The rust of the knife was scraped off and given to Iphiclus in wine for ten days. It restored his virility and enabled him to have a son, Podarces.
Melampus's imprisonment at Phylacus's house lasts nearly a year, during which he is kept in bonds with two attendants, one kind and one cruel.

is_caused_by worms [who reveal that the beam is failing] Melampus heard worms overhead saying that they had gnawed through the beam and warned the attendants to carry him out. The beam then broke and killed the woman, while the man reported what had happened to Phylacus.

restores virility [after drinking rust of the knife in wine] Iphiclus's inability to have children was attributed to the fright and injury associated with Phylacus's knife. Following the vulture's advice, he drank wine containing rust from the knife for ten days, recovered his virility, and had a son.

l: marriage of Bias and Pero, The Library
s: is_arranged_by Neleus [in exchange for recovering the kine] Neleus promised Pero to whoever recovered the kine. After Melampus delivered them to Neleus, Bias received Pero as his bride, and children were born to them.

The story presents the knife's contact with Iphiclus's genitals as causing his loss of virility because the knife had just been used in gelding animals. His cure through drinking the rust of the same knife is described as an example of sympathetic or homoeopathic magic.
Water of life, found between Clashing Rocks that briefly open, is sought and retrieved, then heals Prince Ivan's heroic steed or restores the dead.

l: the two clashing mountains, The Library
s: Two clashing mountains briefly open each day, enclosing water and fountains of life and death; Prince Ivan passes through for water, while a stork loses its tail escaping before they close destructively.

possesses Prince Ivan's heroic steed Prince Ivan is sent to obtain healing and vivifying water preserved between two mountains that open for two or three minutes each day. He rides between the mountains, fills two flasks, and escapes, although the closing cliffs smash the hind legs of his horse; the magic water soon remedies the injury.
Floria, a hero in a Rumanian story, is ordered by a king to procure waters of life and death, seeking a stork’s help after kindness.
The water of death is located with the water of life at fountains beneath mountains that knock against one another. Floria’s helper retrieves some of it in a bottle.

The stork, king of the storks and Floria’s grateful helper, leads the birds to seek the mountains holding the fountains of life and death. An old, maimed stork finds them, fills the two bottles, and escapes after the mountains tear off his tail.

The swallow flies from the mountain’s heart to warn the stork not to enter before noon, then directs him to descend, fill bottles from the ledge between the waters, and escape without touching the mountain or pebbles.

l: the fountains of life and death, The Library
s: The fountains of life and death, two waters at the bottom of mountains that knock together, are reached by the stork during noontide rest and bottled.

l: the modern Greek girl, The Library
s: A modern Greek girl enters a mountain that opens at noon to fetch water of life. As it closes, she cuts her caught skirt with a sword to escape, then uses the water to restore her two brothers from stone.

is_directed_to water of life [by the old woman] The young man is directed by an old woman to a mountain containing many springs and opening every day at noon. He must draw water only from the spring to which a bee leads him, or he will be lost.

is_a hero [in the Eskimo story] Giviok paddles until he reaches two icebergs with a passage that alternately opens and closes. He ventures between them and passes through just before they close, bruising the stern-point of his kayak.

have_between_them a narrow passage [that alternately opens and closes] The two icebergs remain ahead of Giviok when he tries to pass around them, while the passage between them alternately opens and closes. They close together immediately after he passes and bruise the stern-point of his kayak.

Argo, commanded by Jason as admiral, carried Jason and the Argonauts, including Hercules, Orpheus, Peleus, Periclymenus, Phanus, and Palaemon. It reached the river Phasis in Colchis, encountered the Wandering and Clashing Rocks, whose passage cost a dove’s tail, and was later dedicated by Jason to Poseidon at Corinth.

is_a story type [in the author's interpretation] The folk-tale tradition includes stories of precious waters enclosed between closing cliffs or mountains and of heroes or helpers who barely escape. The unit argues that the Clashing Rocks and the voyage of the Argo resemble simple folk-tales more than solar myths.
Christ, in disguise on earth, restores youth, receives confessing Judas as disciple, entrusts him with money, then Judas resumes old evil behavior.

l: Pra T’hong Rat Koma, The Library
s: Pra T’hong Rat Koma, a mythical king of Cambodia, develops leprosy in later years and refuses a learned Brahmin’s proposed cure of death in boiling medicine.

The learned Brahmin offers to cure Pra T’hong Rat Koma by killing and boiling him in medicine, demonstrates it on a dog, then enters the cauldron himself; the king adds all three drugs at once, turning him into a stone statue.
The Shans of Lakon tell a story about Kom-ma Rattsee, a magician, demigod, and doctor, and a decrepit old prince who desired renewed youth.

is_a magician [also a demigod and doctor] Kom-ma Rattsee claimed that his medicines and charms could restore beauty, youth, and life to anyone, even someone dismembered and mangled. He minced the decrepit old prince, boiled the fragments in a magic broth, and restored him as a handsome young man, but later put him back into the pot when the prince repeatedly demanded a second treatment.

l: decrepit old prince of Lakon, The Library
s: remains_in Lakon [after being minced and put into the pot a second time] The decrepit old prince of Lakon was verging on dotage and longed for renewed youth. After being minced and boiled in a magic broth, he became a handsome young man, but his covetousness and persistence led Kom-ma Rattsee to mince him again, leaving him in the pot.

l: Papuans of Geelvink Bay, The Library
s: tell_story_about old Papuan sago seller [on the northern coast of Dutch New Guinea] The Papuans of Geelvink Bay tell of an old man who sold intoxicating sago-palm juice and renewed his youth by means of fire and a magical wand.

l: old Papuan sago seller, The Library
s: An old Papuan sago seller earns a living selling intoxicating sago-palm juice. After catching the Morning Star stealing from his vessels, he receives a magical wand, then throws himself into an iron-wood fire to please his wife and emerges rejuvenated.
Morning Star steals intoxicating juice from an old Papuan sago seller’s vessels, is caught, and ransoms herself by giving him a magical wand that fulfills every wish.

ensures fulfilment of every wish [to its owner] The magical wand given by the Morning Star ensured that its owner’s every wish was fulfilled. The old Papuan sago seller used it in renewing his youth with fire.

is_possible_through fire as a means of rejuvenation [as a conjectured belief reflected in the stories] The unit presents renewal of youth as a transformation achieved through boiling, burning, or magical means. It suggests that such stories reflect a belief that fire has a genial or renovating influence capable of restoring youth and prolonging life.

l: fire as a means of rejuvenation, The Library
s: Fire is associated with rejuvenation in the story of the old Papuan sago seller, who became young after entering glowing embers. The text also connects fire and heat with the Wajagga ceremony intended to prolong a nobleman’s life and with Greek beliefs about roasting babies to make them immortal.

The Wajagga of Mount Kilimandjaro are described as observing a ceremony intended to protect people from sickness and death and to prolong a great man’s life. Their practice involves confining a nobleman and a female companion in a covered trench while a fire burns and food boils above them.
Mount Kilimandjaro is the location of the Wajagga custom called the boiling of a nobleman. The ceremony is presented as an example of using heat to prolong life.

claims_power_to protect people against sickness and death [according to the Wajagga custom] The Wajagga wizard conducts the ceremony of boiling a nobleman. He arranges the trench, fire, pot, and confinement, then spits on the participants and declares that the nobleman will have long life and be protected from death in war and from musket balls.

l: boiling a nobleman ceremony, The Library
s: Nduwmo woika ndu nnini is a Wajagga custom performed for a nobleman to make a name and prolong his life. A nobleman and female companion sweat in a covered trench beneath hearthstones while food boils, then are released and blessed by a wizard.

The Wajagga nobleman undergoes the boiling a nobleman ceremony to make himself a name and prolong his life. He lies in a covered trench beneath a fire and boiling pot, sweats throughout the day, and receives the wizard’s blessing of long life and protection.

Glaucus of Anthedon, a fisherman distinguished from Glaucus son of Minos, discovers a life-giving herb by watching an animal revive, tastes it, becomes immortal, leaps into the sea, and lives there as a marine deity.

Tylon or Tylus is a Lydian legendary hero killed by a serpent beside the Hermus. His sister Moire restores him with the flower of Zeus after seeing it revive a dead serpent; he is associated with Sardes through coin allusions.

Serpent is a reptile believed in Armenia to know magical life-giving herbs and springs. In resurrection stories, it revives a dead or wounded serpent with a herb, teaching humans plants' healing, renewing, and potentially immortal power.

l: Herb, magical, which brings dead to life, The Library
s: A magical herb, also called grass or the flower of Zeus, restores dead creatures to life by contact and heals wounded or severed bodies. Known in varying forms, its power is learned from animals; Armenian belief says eating it confers immortality.

l: resurrection by a magical herb, The Library
s: Resurrection by a magical herb is a recurring ancient-account and folk-tale event in which contact with the herb restores dead people, animals, or severed bodies, often after an observer copies an animal.

l: belief in serpents' knowledge of immortality plants, The Library
s: A popular Armenian belief holds that serpents know life-extending plants and springs; old, sick, or wounded snakes seek them, shed their skins, eat a flower, drink, and regain healing, youth, and immortality.

Oedipus, a legendary figure exposed by his father Laius, arrives in Sphinx-afflicted Thebes after unknowingly killing his father in Phocis and marrying his mother. He is expelled from Thebes and received by Theseus among the Athenians.

is_a tale [containing the same double tragedy as the Oedipus legend] The Finnish tale recounts a prophecy that a newborn boy will kill his father and marry his mother. The boy is abandoned, later fulfills the prophecy unknowingly, and undergoes difficult penance for his crimes.
An elder wizard who knows fate predicts a kid’s death and a peasant’s son killing his father and marrying his mother, repeatedly urging a younger wizard not to help.

is_a wizard [younger of two wizards] The younger wizard proposes to help the she-goat give birth and later offers to help the peasant’s wife during childbirth. The elder wizard prevents him from doing so.

is_married_to peasant’s wife The peasant overhears the wizards’ prophecy and tells his wife, but they do not kill their child. After the kid is eaten by a wolf as predicted, he and his wife wound their son, tie him to a table, and throw him into the sea.

is_married_to peasant The peasant’s wife learns that her unborn son is predicted to kill his father and marry his mother. She joins her husband in abandoning the child at sea and later unknowingly marries him after he has killed her husband.

l: son of the peasant (Finnish tale), The Library
s: A son predicted to kill his father and marry his mother survives wounding and the sea, is raised by an abbot, kills his employer, marries his mother, seeks penance through further killings, and is finally told no more expiation is needed.
The field mistress hires a young man to guard her fields; after he unknowingly kills her husband, she forgives and marries him, then discovers from a scar that he is her son.

is_married_to field mistress [before his death] The field mistress’s husband enters his own field, apparently as a robber, and is struck and killed by the young man guarding it. He is later revealed to be the young man’s father.
A monk who offers penance to a repentant sinner, prescribing an impossible well in rock and a black sheep turned white, then declares no further expiation needed after the sinner kills a gentleman.

contains Ukrainian tale Ukraine is identified as the setting of a variant of the story in which a son unknowingly kills his father, marries his mother, kills her after discovering their relationship, and performs lengthy penance.

contains parricide [committed in ignorance] The Ukrainian tale begins with parents abandoning their son at sea because of a dream predicting his crimes. Raised by sailors, he later kills his father unknowingly, marries his mother, kills her after learning the truth, and ultimately dies after a long penance.

l: father in the Ukrainian tale, The Library
s: is_married_to son in the Ukrainian tale [the son later marries his mother] The father in the Ukrainian tale dreams that his son will kill him, marry his mother, and later kill her. He cuts open the child’s belly and casts him into the sea in a barrel, but later unknowingly employs him and is shot by him while testing his obedience.

l: son in the Ukrainian tale, The Library
s: The son is rescued and raised by sailors, later unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother, then kills her and performs penance involving an apple tree and well.

A priest who imposes an arduous penance: the sinner must plant and water an apple-wood staff until it bears ripe apples. He later confines the sinner in a locked well and declares him saved after keys are recovered from a fish.

tell Kalangs [they tell a story accounting for the tribe’s origin] The Javanese tell a story explaining the origin of the Kalangs in which a woman descended from a sow unknowingly marries her son, while the son kills a dog who is really his father. The text says that such stories about alien peoples may express racial contempt rather than record actual incest.

is_a indigenous tribe of Java The Kalangs are an indigenous tribe of Java whose origin story is told by the Javanese. The text reports that the Javanese associate them with descent from a dog and a pig and with incestuous unions, but cautions that these claims may be hostile inventions.

Judas Iscarioth is a figure in The Golden Legend whose story repeats the Oedipal pattern: abandoned at sea, he rises in Pontius Pilate’s court, unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother, becomes a disciple of Christ after learning the truth, then returns to evil through the money bag.

Cyborea, married to Ruben Simeon and mother of Judas Iscarioth, dreams her son will destroy the family, abandons him at sea, then unknowingly marries him after he kills Ruben Simeon and reveals their bond.
governs Judea [as governor] Pontius Pilate appoints Judas Iscarioth to a high office. He gives Judas the property of the man Judas killed and the man’s widow, Cyborea, in marriage.

Judas’s father owns a garden in Jerusalem. While resisting Judas’s attempt to obtain apples for Pontius Pilate, he is struck on the head and killed by Judas without either recognizing their relationship.

is_a crime [in the Oedipus-related stories] Parricide is presented as one of the two crimes committed unknowingly by Oedipus and as a recurring element in the Finnish, Ukrainian, Javanese, and Judas Iscarioth stories.

is_a crime [in the Oedipus-related stories] Incest with a mother is presented alongside parricide in the Oedipus legend and in several related tales. The text rejects the view that such traditions necessarily preserve memories of an earlier widespread custom.

Kwakiutl beliefs and stories center on twins as salmon in human form who can bring salmon, as shown by Salmon-Maker, who withdraws salmon after disrespect. Another story follows Born-to-be-the-Sun: conceived through sunlight, he ascends to the Sun, tries to replace it, causes destruction, and is thrown back to earth.
Baganda believed twins were sent and specially protected by Mukasa; visits from twins and their parents were welcomed for blessings, children, and increased herds and crops.

requires twins [the clan does not sow until the twins are brought to the field] The Basoga attributed the birth of twins to the god Gasani and built a shrine near the twins' home where offerings were made, including by barren women seeking children. In central Busoga, seed was not sown until twins had been brought to the field, and the twins' mother had to sow her seed first.

Twins are associated in the unit with powers of fertility, abundance, and attraction, especially over animals, salmon, plants, crops, and seed. In other traditions they are treated as dangerous or unlucky, and their birth can be believed to cause drought, famine, crop failure, disease, or cattle deaths.

After twins’ birth, parents remain secluded and observe rituals for two years, avoiding fresh salmon. They are credited with fertilizing or abundance-producing power, attracting salmon among the Nootkas and receiving blessing-seeking visits or offerings among the Baganda and Bateso.

l: fertilizing power of twins, The Library
s: A rare, exceptional belief that twins, and sometimes their parents, quicken or multiply living things: cattle and crops in some societies, and also salmon, livestock, children, plantains, and seed.

The birth of twins is welcomed and celebrated in some societies as a sign of fertility, abundance, or a good salmon year. In others it is regarded with horror as an omen of drought, famine, crop failure, epidemics, sickness among cattle, or other misfortune.

is_a fish Salmon are believed by the Tsimshian, Nootkas, and Kwakiutl to be attracted, increased, or produced through the power of twins and their parents. The Kwakiutl story says that salmon disappear when Salmon-Maker leaves after being treated disrespectfully.

The Baganda believed that twins and their parents could multiply crops. In contrast, the birth of twins was believed in some places to portend crop failure, and women who had borne twins among the Bassari were forbidden to enter cornfields during sowing and harvest.

Among the Basoga, a field was not sown until the twins had been brought to it, with food and all the seed placed before them. The mother of twins was required to sow her seed before other members of her clan sowed theirs.

l: exposure or killing of twins, The Library
s: is_a custom [practised in some societies because twins are regarded as harmful or unlucky] In some societies twins were exposed or killed because their birth was believed to bring misfortune. In Nias, one or both twins were sometimes left to perish, while in Ngura twins were ordered to be killed and thrown into water to prevent droughts, famines, floods, or other afflictions.

is_a folk-tale [modern Greek story] The Cretan tale concerns a young man who marries a sea-maiden after holding her through several transformations until cock-crow. She later speaks when he threatens their child, then vanishes and lives near the sea-nymphs' cave with her baby.

is_a lyre player [in the Cretan tale] The young man plays the lyre beautifully and is carried off by sea nymphs to their cave. He follows advice to seize a sea-maiden by the hair, marries her, and later loses her after threatening to throw their child into the fire.

A sea-maiden changes into a dog, serpent, camel, and fire while a young man holds her. After the cock crows she marries him, remains silent for a year, and bears a son. When he threatens the child, she speaks, leaves him, and settles at a spring after the Nereids reject her.

l: Peleus and Thetis marriage, The Library
s: Peleus and Thetis’ marriage is a silent, localized supernatural-bride tale, possibly including an immortality ritual, whose separation follows the bride’s return to her former home.

The silence of the bride is interpreted as possibly recalling customs that impose silence on brides after marriage. The unit gives examples of the Tedas bride, who remains silent for seven days, and the Wabende wife, who does not speak to her husband for several days until he gives her a present.
The immortality ritual is the conjectured act in which Thetis places her child on the fire to make him immortal. Peleus interrupts and reproaches her, believing that she is murdering the infant.

is_a popular tale type [in comparative folklore] The Swan Maiden type features supernatural females who temporarily assume human form, are constrained into marriage by the concealment of their skins, and later recover those skins and return to their original life. The marriage of Peleus and Thetis is presented as belonging to this familiar type.
Swan Maiden is a fairy wife who becomes a beautiful maiden, marries and bears a child after her bird-skin is hidden, then recovers it and flies back to her old life.

is_a localized version of a folk-tale [according to W. Mannhardt] The Peleus saga is discussed as a popular tale that W. Mannhardt studied in detail. The unit states that the modern Cretan story was probably an independent folk-tale rather than a reminiscence of the story of the marriage of Thetis.

l: fish-skin or animal-skin motif, The Library
s: causes fairy wife’s departure [when the wife discovers and resumes the cast skin] The fish-skin or animal-skin motif involves a supernatural spouse who removes a fish, bird, beast, or other skin to live as a human. When the hidden skin is discovered, the spouse resumes its original form and returns to its former home, often after an act of unkindness or a cruel taunt.

is_a animal skin [in Faroe Islands and Shetland tales] The seal-skin or ham is the covering that allows seals or mermaids in the Faré Islands and Shetland to take human form. Men who hide it can marry the transformed female, but when she finds and resumes it, she returns to the sea.

l: Indian tribes of North-western America, The Library
s: tell Phaethon myth [in a closely resembling story] Indian tribes of North-western America tell stories resembling the Greek story of Phaethon and the chariot of the Sun. Their versions include a child of the Sun who takes over the Sun’s course and causes the earth to burn.

tell Bella Coola Sun myth [in British Columbia] The Bella Coola Indians tell of a woman who reaches the house of the Sun and bears his son, Totqoaya. Their story includes the boy’s attempt to replace the Sun, the burning of the earth, and his transformation into a mink.

Totqoaya, the Sun’s son in the Bella Coola story, is mocked by other children, ascends to heaven, takes the Sun’s torches and burns the earth, then is thrown down by the Sun and transformed into a mink.

Born-to-be-the-Sun, the Sun’s Kwakiutl child, is mocked, taught to follow the Sun’s path, then takes the Sun’s place. He sweeps away clouds and burns the world before the Sun pursues him and throws him down through the sky.

is_based_on Greek literature [according to the author’s assessment] The Phaethon myth concerns the Sun’s son, who proves his parentage by driving the solar chariot. His failure to control it nearly destroys heaven and earth, and he dies after Jupiter strikes him with a thunderbolt.

l: Bella Coola Sun myth, The Library
s: The Bella Coola Sun myth tells how a woman reaches the Sun’s house, bears his son Totqoaya, and later returns to earth. Totqoaya takes the Sun’s torches, burns the earth, and is transformed into a mink.

The Kwakiutl Sun myth tells how Born-to-be-the-Sun, mocked for having no father, climbs to the Sun and temporarily takes his place. He ignores warnings, causes the world to burn, and is thrown down through the sky.

are_used_by Sun [to regulate the heat of the day] In the Bella Coola story, the Sun uses one torch in the morning, adds more until noon, and extinguishes them in the afternoon. Totqoaya lights all the torches too soon, making the earth unbearably hot and causing woods to burn, rocks to crack, and people to die.
In the Bella Coola version, the Sun throws Totqoaya down to earth and declares that he shall henceforth be a mink. The text notes that the unlucky hero becomes a mink in the Indian versions.

l: house of the Sun, The Library
s: The house of the Sun is the destination of Phaethon and of the Indian Sun’s children. It is portrayed as a radiant or fiery dwelling in which the Sun receives and instructs the would-be successors.

l: burning of the earth, The Library
s: The burning of the earth results when Phaethon drives too low or when the Indian Sun’s children use the Sun’s instruments improperly. The destruction includes burning forests and trees, boiling waters, cracked rocks, and widespread danger to people.

l: metamorphosis into a mink, The Library
s: In the Bella Coola account, Totqoaya’s failed attempt to control the Sun’s torches ends with his being changed into a mink. The text states that the hero appears sooner or later as a mink in the Indian versions.

European influence is offered as one possible explanation for the similarities between the Greek and Indian stories. The text says there is no evidence sufficient to determine whether this explanation is correct.

Independent invention is offered as another possible explanation for the similarities between the Greek and Indian stories. The text says that the available evidence does not permit a firm choice between it and European influence.

is_first_to_meet Idomeneus [on Idomeneus's return from Troy] Idomeneus's son was, according to Servius, the first person to meet Idomeneus after the vow. Idomeneus sacrificed him or attempted to do so; the First Vatican Mythographer instead names a daughter as the victim.

is_first_to_meet Idomeneus [in the First Vatican Mythographer's variation] Idomeneus's daughter is identified by the First Vatican Mythographer, rather than his son, as the first person he met and sacrificed or attempted to sacrifice.
Pestilence follows Idomeneus's sacrifice or attempted sacrifice of his child and is seen as divine judgment, causing his banishment.

Idomeneus's banishment followed the pestilence in Servius's account, because the people regarded his treatment of his child as cruel. In Apollodorus's different account, Leucus expelled him after seizing ten cities of Crete.

Maeander, son of Cercaphus and Anaxibia, wars against Pessinus and vows the Mother of the Gods the first person to congratulate him if victorious. He sacrifices Archelaus, his wife, and daughter in fulfilment, then throws himself into the river that bears his name.

vows_to_sacrifice human sacrifice [if delivered from the Ammonites] Jephthah vowed to the Lord that he would offer as a burnt offering whoever first came out of his house to meet him if he defeated the Ammonites. The unit interprets the vow as intending human sacrifice from the outset.
Jephthah's daughter was the first person to meet him after his victory. Jephthah fulfilled his vow by doing to her what he had promised.

is_intended_by Jephthah [in the interpretation of the Hebrew, Septuagint, and Vulgate texts] The unit treats the vows of Maeander and Jephthah as promises of human sacrifice rather than ordinary animal offerings. It also connects them with Idomeneus's sacrifice or attempted sacrifice of his child.

is_from Hesse [a German story] In a German story from Hesse, a man promises a lion whatever first meets him at home in exchange for a singing, soaring lark. His youngest daughter meets him first and goes to the lion, who proves to be an enchanted prince and marries her.

demands youngest daughter (German folktale) [as the first person meeting the girl's father at home] The lion threatens to devour a man who tries to take his singing, soaring lark. It accepts the promise of whatever first meets the man at home, but is later revealed to be an enchanted prince who marries the man's daughter.

is_loved_by literal value: her father [as his favourite child] The youngest daughter is the man's favourite child and the first person to meet him after he obtains the singing, soaring lark. She bravely agrees to go to the lion, who turns out to be an enchanted prince and becomes her husband.

is_an_enchanted_prince literal value: enchanted prince [in the Lorraine story] The white wolf in the Lorraine story owns a castle and its talking roses. It spares a man on condition that he bring the first person he meets at home, receives the man's youngest daughter, and is revealed as a fairy condemned to appear as a wolf by day; after the daughter reveals his secret, he falls dead.

The youngest daughter is the first person her father meets after he obtains a talking rose from the white wolf. She willingly goes with him to the castle, where the wolf promises to marry her, but she later reveals his secret and causes him to fall dead.

is_a literal value: youngest daughter [of the Lithuanian king] The princess in the Lithuanian story is the youngest and fairest of a king's three daughters. Her father promises her to a white wolf after obtaining a hood of living flowers, and the wolf carries her away before revealing himself as an enchanted prince who eventually marries her.

A serpent demands the first person a merchant meets at home after taking a singing and playing leaf. The merchant’s youngest daughter goes to it; later revealed as an enchanted nobleman, it marries her when its spell is broken.

The youngest daughter asks her father for a leaf that dances, sings, and plays. She is the first person to meet him after he takes one from the serpent's garden, goes willingly to the serpent, and marries it after it becomes a handsome young man.

In the Hanoverian story, an enchanted prince disguised as a black poodle promises a king a tinkling lion-leaf for what first meets him, carries off the youngest daughter, and is revealed when she burns its dog-skin.
Schleswig-Holstein is a place where two stories of the same general type, a first and second, were recorded.

features king (first Schleswig-Holstein story) It concerns a king who promises a big bear whatever first meets him at his castle in exchange for a golden jingle-jangle. The king's youngest daughter is eventually sent to the bear, who is transformed into a rich and handsome prince and marries her.

A king with three daughters owns a golden spinning-wheel and reel. Seeking a golden jingle-jangle, he promises the big bear whatever first meets him at his castle, unsuccessfully substitutes two other girls, and finally sends his youngest daughter.

l: youngest daughter (first Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library
s: A youngest daughter desires golden jingle-jangle, meets a big bear, is sent to him by her father, visits home with him, hurts his paw, and marries the prince he becomes.

l: big bear (first Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library
s: Big bear guards golden jingle-jangles on a great tall tree and trades one to a king for what first meets him at his castle. Rejecting substitutes, he accepts the youngest daughter; when she treads on his paw, the spell breaks and he becomes a rich, handsome prince.
A rich, handsome prince, the big bear’s assumed form, emerges after the youngest daughter treads on his paw and marries her.
is_located_on great tall tree [in the forest] It is the youngest daughter's requested present. A big bear gives one to the king in exchange for whatever first meets him at his castle.

features daughter (second Schleswig-Holstein story) It concerns a king who promises a little black man whatever first comes out of his house to meet him. His daughter is the first to appear and is taken away by a white wolf, who turns out to be an enchanted prince.

offers_guidance_to king (first Schleswig-Holstein story) [in exchange for whatever first came out of the king’s house] He appears to a king who has lost his way and offers to guide him home if the king promises to give him whatever first comes out of the king's house to meet him.
She is the first to run out of the king's house when he returns. She willingly goes away after learning that she has been promised, and a white wolf fetches her.
He fetches the king's daughter after she becomes bound by the king's promise. He turns out to be an enchanted prince and marries her when the spell binding him is broken.

l: enchanted prince (second Schleswig-Holstein story), The Library
s: He is the form revealed by the white wolf after the spell binding him is broken. He marries the king's daughter.

loses_way_in wood He loses his way in a wood and meets a poodle that offers to guide him home in exchange for whatever first comes out of his house to meet him. His daughter is the first to appear, and the apparent calamity ends in her marriage with a prince.
It meets a nobleman who has lost his way and offers to guide him home if he will give it whatever first comes out of his house to meet him.

is_loved_by king [more than the other daughters] She is the king's youngest and dearest daughter and is the first living thing to meet him when he returns home. Her father eventually sends her into the forest, and she is happily wedded to the man in the grey cloak.

l: man in the grey cloak, The Library
s: is_enchanted_as enchanted prince or nobleman (Swedish story) [as usual] He repeatedly meets a king who is lost in the forest and says that the king must give him the first living thing that meets him at home. He sends the king's two elder daughters back with rich presents and later becomes the husband of the youngest daughter.

l: enchanted prince or nobleman (Swedish story), The Library
s: An enchanted prince or nobleman, revealed as the man in the grey cloak, owns a fine castle and, after adventures, happily marries the youngest daughter.
A rash vow binds a person and, in most folk-tales, ends fortunately with a princely husband and wedded bliss.

The stories involve promises to give a supernatural or animal figure whatever first meets or comes out to greet a returning man. The text suggests that such vows may preserve a reminiscence of a custom that in real life could end in sacrifice.

l: sacrifice of the victim, The Library
s: occurs_at altar [in real life under the suspected custom] The text contrasts the happy endings of the folk-tales with the possibility that the promised victim was sacrificed or killed in real life.

l: custom of sacrificial vows, The Library
s: is_reminisced_by legends [possibly] The stories are said to preserve a possible reminiscence of a custom in which a vow could end with the sacrifice of the victim at the altar.

l: Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus, The Library
s: The Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus is an ancient story type that survives in oral tradition and has modern versions among many widely separated peoples. Its central pattern involves a one-eyed giant’s cave, the capture and devouring of people, tricks with names such as “Nobody” and “Myself,” the giant’s blinding, and escape through or among a flock of sheep. Closely resembling versions are recorded in Sicily, Mingrelia, the Caucasus, Oghuz traditions, Armenia, Russia, and among the Lapps. Its common source may be the Odyssey, or more probably an older folk-tale incorporated by Homer.

John of Haute-Seille was a monk of the Cistercian Abbey of Haute-Seille in Lorraine who wrote Dolopathos in or soon after 1184; his Polyphemus account apparently drew on oral tradition rather than the Homeric narrative.

l: Dolopathos sive de Rege et Septem Sapientibus, The Library
s: Dolopathos is a mediaeval Latin collection of tales by John of Haute-Seille, dedicated to Bertrand, Bishop of Metz. Based directly or indirectly on The Book of Sindibad and perhaps oral tradition, it includes a divergent Polyphemus tale: a famous robber deceives and blinds a giant, involving a severed finger.

A famous aged robber, wealthy from robbery, resolves to practice virtue. He recounts being captured with fellow robbers by a giant, blinding it, escaping among sheep, and cutting off its finger with a magic ring.

is_captured_by Polyphemus [with nine others accompanying him] The hundred robbers went to the giant's dwelling to steal his gold and silver while he was absent. The giant and nine others captured them, divided them among themselves, and the famous robber and nine companions were taken to the giant whose wealth they had stolen.

The giant's cave, a solitary prison about twenty miles from human abodes, is masonry-enclosed with an iron-barred sole exit; a famous robber escapes by hiding among the giant's sheep and passing out with the flock.

Polyphemus’s gold ring, drawn from his finger as a reward, bewitches the robber into revealing himself; to escape, the hero severs the finger wearing it and throws finger and ring back to the blind giant.
The giant's blinding is a stratagem: a robber, posing as a doctor, gains consent to treat aching eyes, then pours a boiling harmful mixture over the giant's head, leaving him completely blind.

l: the hero's escape from the giant, The Library
s: The hero escapes the blinded giant by first hiding on the roof, hanging from a beam, then disguising himself in a ram’s fleece and passing with the flock as the giant counts sheep. A bewitched ring delays complete escape until he sacrifices a severed finger.

Oral tradition is presented as the likely source of the unusual features in the Dolopathos version. The recurrence of those features in popular versions supports the view that John of Haute-Seille drew on oral tradition rather than solely on the Odyssey.

Conall Cra Bhuidhe is a man and father of Conall's sons. As a young lad he hunts on his father's land. Later he and his sons try to steal the King of Lochlann's brown horse, are caught, and he saves their lives by recounting adventures against a one-eyed giant, marked by his severed finger.

rules Lochlann The King of Lochlann catches Conall Cra Bhuidhe and his sons while they are attempting to steal his brown horse. He would have hanged them, but Conall saves their lives by telling his story.

Conall's giant is a one-eyed giant who owns goats, their leading buck, and a talking ring. He keeps goats in a cave and intends to eat Conall, but Conall blinds him, escapes in the buck's skin, and causes him to drown pursuing the ring.

number two dozen Conall’s goats are kept by the giant and are released one by one while the giant, unable to see, feels them at the cave’s entrance. Conall uses the release of the goats to escape while disguised in the buck’s skin.
Conall’s buck is at the head of the giant’s goats. Conall kills it, flays it bag-wise, and uses its skin and position to pass the giant at the cave entrance.

l: talking ring (Conall's giant's ring), The Library
s: is_a talking ring The giant gives Conall a ring that answers when the giant asks where it is. Conall cuts off the finger bearing the ring and throws it into deep water; the giant follows the ring’s voice into the water and drowns.

Tartaro is a one-eyed colossus, shepherd, and hunter of people, with an old witch for a mother. He eats one sheep daily before human victims. A young man blinds him, escapes in a sheep’s skin, and defeats his pursuit by cutting off the finger bearing Tartaro’s ring.
A young man captured by Tartaro sees him eat a sheep, blinds him with a red-hot spit, escapes hidden in a sheep’s skin, and severs his finger to evade a location-revealing ring.

is_a talking ring [it cries out when worn] Tartaro’s ring is given to the escaping young man as a supposed remembrance of his escape. It cries out that the young man has it, so he cuts off the finger bearing it and throws it away.

Basa-Jaun is a hairy, one-eyed giant who owns sheep and eats one soldier. After trying to catch the other, he is blinded; the survivor escapes in a sheep’s skin, cuts off his talking ring-bearing finger, and causes him to drown.
A soldier traveling with a companion survives Basa-Jaun eating the companion, blinds Basa-Jaun, escapes among sheep in a skin, and removes a location-calling ring.
A giant captures three brothers and eats two, then hunts the youngest after being blinded; a revealing ring betrays the youth until it is thrown into water, drowning the giant.

is_a brothers [three shepherds captured by the giant] The three brothers are taken by the Rumanian giant after answering his calls at night. The eldest and second brothers are eaten, while the youngest survives and escapes.

is_a youngest of three brothers The youngest brother survives after the Rumanian giant eats his two brothers. He blinds the giant, escapes disguised in a ram’s skin, and cuts off his finger to throw the talking ring into the water, causing the giant to drown.

Italian Eye-in-his-forehead is a one-eyed giant with an enchanted ring who eats Big Brother and plans to eat Little Brother, until Little Brother blinds him, escapes, and cuts off the ring-bearing finger.
is_a brother [older brother of Little Brother] Big Brother is chosen by lot to be eaten first by Italian Eye-in-his-forehead. The giant roasts him on a spit and eats him.

is_a brother [younger brother of Big Brother] Little Brother escapes Italian Eye-in-his-forehead after pretending to eat Big Brother, blinding the giant, and disguising himself in a ram’s skin. He cuts off the finger bearing the enchanted ring and throws it at the giant.

l: John of Haute-Seille's version, The Library
s: is_a version of the story John of Haute-Seille’s version is identified as having distinctive features that recur in the West Highland story and related versions. The unit does not separately recount its plot.

is_a story type Ulysses and Polyphemus is the story pattern to which the unit’s West Highland, Basque, Rumanian, and Italian tales are compared. Its recurring features include a one-eyed giant, blinding, escape among sheep or goats, and in several versions a ring that leads to the giant’s death.

A Florentine traveler journeys through wood with a curate and workman, works for a giant who kills workers, blinds him with boiling oil, escapes by cutting off a ring-trapped finger, and returns exhausted to Florence, unwilling to travel or recount adventures.
A clergyman accepts a curacy in the giant’s parish, where the giant shows him leaves, beheads him with a scimitar, and buries him.
is_offered job [in the giant’s workshop] The workman accepts a position in the giant’s workshop. The giant shows him some leaves and then cuts off his head with a scimitar in the same chamber.

l: giant in the Italian story, The Library
s: A giant with a fine palace, parish, workshop, marble table, and one defective eye offers jobs to a man of Florence, a curate, and a workman, then kills the latter two. Blinded by boiling oil, he pursues the man carrying the table and gives him a ring that turns his finger to marble.
Boiling oil treatment is intended for the giant’s defective eye: a man of Florence puts herb in oil, heats it to boiling, ties the giant to a marble table, and pours it over both eyes, blinding him.

l: escape from the giant, The Library
s: The man of Florence blinds the giant; a thrown ring turns his finger to marble, immobilizing him. He cuts it off with a knife and escapes while the giant, burdened by marble table, cannot catch him.

l: characteristic escape by sheep or sheepskin, The Library
s: An episode of the Polyphemus story, it has a captive escape hidden beneath, clinging to, or clad in sheep or ram skin; it recurs in variants but is absent from Pisa’s Italian version and both Arabian Nights versions.
A Serbian priest travels through a mountainous region with his scholar, enters a one-eyed giant’s cave, is judged fatter, killed, and roasted over a fire.

A Serbian scholar travels with a priest, is forced by a giant to take roasted priest’s flesh but secretly spits it out, blinds the sleeping giant, escapes disguised in a ram’s skin among sheep, and loses a finger freeing himself from the giant’s staff.
A cave holds a one-eyed giant, fire, and sheep; a stone blocks its mouth, but a scholar escapes disguised in a ram’s skin.

l: one-eyed giant in the Serbian story, The Library
s: A one-eyed giant with sheep in his cave admits a priest and Serbian scholar, seals them in with a huge stone, and roasts the priest. The scholar blinds him with a sharpened stick, escapes, and is pursued until the giant falls into water.
A Serbian priest, selected by a one-eyed giant as the fatter traveller, is knocked on the head, put on a spit over fire, roasted, and tasted by the scholar.
are_kept_in cave [many sheep] The sheep are in the cave with the one-eyed giant. The scholar hides among them while wearing a ram’s skin and slips out when the giant releases the sheep one by one.
A ram’s-skin disguise worn by a Serbian scholar lets him mingle with sheep in a cave, pass the entrance, and escape from a giant.

resembles Esthonian story [in some points] The Russian story concerns a smith who searches for evil, encounters Likho, and escapes by disguising himself as a sheep. It is said to belong to the same class as related stories from Esthonia and Lapland.

Smith, a Russian story figure, seeks Likho to find evil, meets a tailor, tricks and attacks the one-eyed woman at Likho’s cottage, escapes disguised as a sheep, loses his hand to a golden-handled hatchet, and returns to a Russian village.
is_killed_by one-eyed woman (Likho's cottage) [at the cottage] The tailor joins the smith in searching for evil. The one-eyed woman cuts his throat, trusses him, and puts him in the oven.
Likho is identified with evil in the Russian story and appears as a tall, crooked, one-eyed woman. She pursues the smith after he escapes and causes his hand to stick to a golden-handled hatchet.
A one-eyed woman lives in a large, bare, squalid cottage in a dark forest, kills the tailor, tries to attack the smith, and is tricked.

resembles Russian story [in some points] The Esthonian story concerns a Barn-carl who tricks the devil by pretending to cast eyes. Its use of the name “Myself” is said to resemble Ulysses’ use of “Nobody” against Polyphemus.
Barn-carl, a farm-servant responsible for barns and corn, tells the devil he casts eyes, binds him, pours molten lead on his eyes, and says “Myself” did it.
The devil, bound and blinded with molten lead, seeks new eyes from the Barn-carl, flees past ploughmen blaming “Myself,” and dies from the replacement eyes.
“Myself” is the name the Barn-carl gives, enabling him to truthfully say “Myself” blinded the devil after pouring molten lead into his eyes.

resembles Ulysses and Polyphemus story [more closely than the preceding variants] The Lapp tale concerns four Lapps who enter a giant’s cave, blind the giant with molten lead, and escape disguised in goat skins. It resembles the Homeric story of Ulysses and Polyphemus more closely than the Russian and Esthonian stories do.

lose_way_in mountains and hills [while seeking their reindeer] Four Lapps lose their way, enter a giant’s cave, and hide after eating his beef. They blind the giant with molten lead, escape in the skins of billy-goats with gold and silver, and leave the giant unable to find them.

The giant dwells in a cave with over a hundred goats and stored gold and silver. After capturing Lapps found inside, he is deceived into using molten lead as eye-salve, blinded, and loses them as they escape disguised as goats.

The giant’s cave has silver walls and a roof, a large hearth, a kettle, more than a hundred goats, and stores of gold and silver. The Lapps hide there, blind the giant, and escape through its entrance in goat skins.
Nobody is the name a Lapp gives a giant; after blinding the giant, the Lapp’s name makes the giant’s neighbor refuse help when he says Nobody hurt him.

is_a Lapp tale [a variant of the preceding story] The Lapp variant concerns Slyboots and a Stalo who tries to fatten him before eating him. It repeats the blinding trick and ends with Slyboots escaping from the sheepfold in the skin of a ram.
Slyboots, a Lapp youngest-son figure, defeats a Stalo by blinding him with molten lead, cooks his dog, frees sheep, disguises himself in a ram’s skin, and escapes the fold.

Stalo is a householder who owns a house, kitchen, sheep, and old dog, and keeps Slyboots to fatten and eat. Slyboots blinds Stalo with molten lead, deceives him with dog meat, and escapes in a ram’s skin.
The Stalo’s sheep are kept in a fold and are released one by one. Slyboots kills and skins the big ram, then uses its skin to disguise himself while escaping.

is_a tale [of the same general type as the Homeric story] The Finnish tale concerns the poor ostler Gylpho, who attempts to free three spellbound king’s daughters from an underground cave. It includes a one-eyed rock-spirit who is blinded with a heated poker.
Gylpho, a poor ostler, seeks to free three princesses, thrusts a red-hot poker into Kammo’s eye, then hews off the spirit’s head.

Kammo is an old rock-spirit with a great horn, a single dim eyelashed eye, and an iron poker for the fire; he smells human flesh until Gylpho blinds his eye with a red-hot poker and cuts off his head.
The one-eyed giant in the Karelian story guards a castle and is blinded at night by the hero. The hero then hides under a sheep and escapes when the giant sends the flock out to graze.

is_from Lithuania The Lithuanian tale tells of sailors who enter a giant’s underground house after lifting a stone covering its entrance. They blind the giant with a heated iron spit and escape under sheep, though the giant’s thrown rocks damage their ship and kill some crew members.

leads ship’s crew [on the island] The skipper lands on the island with his crew and devises their escape from the giant. He heats an iron spit, helps ram it into the giant’s eye, and later hides under the old tup to leave with the sheep.

The ship’s crew enters the giant’s cave and loses one member when the giant swallows him. The surviving crew helps blind the giant and escapes under the sheep, but some members are killed when a rock strikes the ship.

l: giant of the island, The Library
s: A one-eyed giant living in a vast cave beneath a mountain on an island swallows a sailor, is blinded with his iron spit, then throws rocks at the departing ship.

belongs_to giant of the island [kept in the cave] The sheep flock belongs to the island giant and provides the sailors with a means of escape. The sailors tie themselves beneath the sheep and pass out of the cave when the flock leaves.
The Yorkshire giant lives at a mill, grinds men’s bones for bread, has one eye and a favourite dog; Jack blinds him, then escapes disguised in the dog’s hide.
Jack, servant of the Yorkshire giant for many years, leaves for Topcliffe Fair, takes the giant’s knife, blinds him, kills his dog, and escapes beneath its hide.

is_from Brittany One Breton version tells of a young man who blinds a one-eyed giant with a pistol and escapes beneath a sheep. Another Breton version concerns Bihanic, who steals a giant’s treasures and escapes after killing the giantess cook.
A young man returns from La Vendée wealthy, enters a one-eyed giant’s hut, blinds him, escapes hidden under a sheep, then sells it.
